text: It is worth remembering who that wall was built against.
One of the most prominent Black Chicagoans of these years was Fannie Barrier Williams.
She had been the first Black woman admitted to the Chicago Woman's Club, a founder of Black women's organizations, and a writer who pressed the city and the nation to open its doors.
She was exactly the kind of accomplished, settled, professional neighbor the club claimed it did not want.
The color line did not ask what you had achieved.
To understand why white Hyde Park reacted with that much force, you have to look at what was happening to the city around it.
Across the South, Black families were leaving sharecropping, lynching, and Jim Crow, drawn north by wartime jobs in the packinghouses, the steel mills, and the rail yards.
Many of them came up the Illinois Central line that ran straight into Chicago.
The Chicago Defender, the city's great Black newspaper, fed the movement directly.
Its publisher, Robert Abbott, printed train schedules and job listings and called for a Great Northern Drive in the spring of 1917.
Pullman porters carried the paper south along the rail lines, and it was read aloud in barbershops and churches across the cotton country.
